query: AlCrFeNiSi belongs to a high-entropy-alloy family developed to combine properties that traditional single-principal-element alloys often cannot achieve simultaneously. Earlier research sought stable solid solutions and adjusted HEA compositions to target particular properties, but tradeoffs persisted: the CoCrFeMnNi system has limited wear and corrosion resistance, manganese can promote oxidation and oxide spallation, and cobalt-containing systems raise cost and processability concerns. Conventional bulk fabrication can cause compositional segregation during cooling, whereas mainstream metallic additive-manufacturing techniques can generate residual thermal stresses that impair mechanical performance and increase processing complexity. Given cobalt-free AlCrFeNiSi powder feedstock, what single intervention could improve mechanical integrity while limiting segregation, residual stress, and defect formation? State one hypothesis containing the intervention, its causal mechanism, a quantitative or directional outcome relative to conventionally fabricated AlCrFeNiSi, the processing and test boundaries of validity, the prior evidence supporting it, and a decisive experiment that could falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Preheating the build substrate during laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) of cobalt‐free AlCrFeNiSi powder feedstock will reduce thermal gradients and slow cooling rates. This intervention is expected to promote homogeneous solute redistribution, diminish compositional segregation, lower residual thermal stresses, and minimize defect formation, thereby improving the alloy’s mechanical integrity.
generation.material_initial_state: Cobalt‐free AlCrFeNiSi high-entropy-alloy powder feedstock prepared for LPBF additive manufacturing.
generation.intervention: Implement a controlled high-temperature preheating of the build substrate (targeting a range of about 500–700 °C) during LPBF processing.
generation.conditions: LPBF processing in an inert atmosphere with all parameters (laser power, scanning speed, layer thickness) constant except for the substrate temperature. Mechanical and microstructural evaluations performed at room temperature on specimens produced with versus without substrate preheating.
generation.structural_mediator: Reduced thermal gradients and slower cooling facilitate more uniform grain growth and solute distribution, thereby minimizing the formation of concentration gradients, porosity, and residual stress build-up.
generation.mechanism: Preheating the substrate decreases the temperature differential between the melt pool and the build platform, which slows the cooling rate. This slower solidification process reduces compositional segregation at grain boundaries and residual stress accumulation while also limiting defect formation (such as porosity) typically induced by rapid thermal cycles.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to conventionally processed samples (with ambient substrate temperature), samples fabricated with substrate preheating will show a more homogeneous microstructure with less segregation, reduced residual stresses (observable by XRD), fewer processing defects, and improved mechanical properties such as higher ductility and strength.
generation.baseline: Conventionally processed AlCrFeNiSi via LPBF that employs ambient temperature substrates, which tend to develop higher thermal gradients, more pronounced segregation, residual stresses, and defects.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies specifically to additive manufacturing via LPBF within the substrate preheating temperature range of 500–700 °C. It is limited to the processing of cobalt‐free AlCrFeNiSi and may not directly translate to bulk casting or alternative manufacturing routes.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal preheating temperature and the exact quantitative improvements in mechanical properties remain to be experimentally validated; there may also be tradeoffs such as potential grain coarsening at higher preheating temperatures.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of AlCrFeNiSi specimens using LPBF: one with the build substrate preheated to 500–700 °C and one using an ambient temperature substrate. Ensure that all other processing parameters remain identical. Post-fabrication, analyze the microstructure via electron microscopy and perform XRD measurements for residual stresses. Conduct mechanical testing (e.g., tensile tests) to compare strength and ductility.
measurements: Electron microscopy to assess grain size, segregation, and defect density
XRD analysis to quantify residual stress levels
Tensile testing to measure yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, and ductility
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the preheated samples do not exhibit statistically significant reductions in residual stresses, segregation, and defect density, as well as no improvement in mechanical properties, compared to the ambient substrate control, then the hypothesis is rejected.
